Advanced
ad-vanst'
v. (raised to rank or honour; promoted)
Old French avancer, to move forward, from Latin ab ante. In the Authorized Version the verb is always about being lifted into place by somebody else — and Scripture is careful about who does the lifting.

Biblical Definition

Samuel puts the doctrine in one sentence at the end of his public ministry: “It is the LORD that advanced Moses and Aaron, and that brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt” (1Sa 12:6). The two greatest men in Israel's history were not self-made; they were advanced, and by the same hand that brought the nation out. Against that stands the book of Esther, which uses the word three times and makes it the hinge of the plot. “King Ahasuerus promote[d] Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes” (Est 3:1). Haman then recites his own promotion to his friends: “all the things wherein the king had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes and servants of the king” (Est 5:11) — and adds that all this availeth him nothing so long as Mordecai sits at the gate. A man advanced above every prince in the empire was made miserable by one man who would not bow. And the book closes with the reversal: “the declaration of the greatness of Mordecai, whereunto the king advanced him” (Est 10:2). The same verb, the same king, the opposite man. God's name never appears in Esther, and His hand is on every page.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines advance as to raise to a higher rank, to promote; to forward, to accelerate growth; and advanced as promoted, raised to a higher rank.

expand to see more

ADVANCE, v.t. To bring forward; to move further in front.

1. To promote; to raise to a higher rank; as, to advance one to the rank of a general.

2. To improve or make better, which is considered as a moving forward.

ADVANCED, pp. Moved forward; promoted; improved; furnished beforehand.

PROMOTION, n. Advancement in place or in honor; exaltation in rank.

Key Scripture

1Sa 12:6 — "And Samuel said unto the people, It is the LORD that advanced Moses and Aaron, and that brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt."

Est 5:11 — "And Haman told them of the glory of his riches, and the multitude of his children, and all the things wherein the king had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes and servants of the king."

Est 3:1 — "After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him."

Est 10:2 — "And all the acts of his power and of his might, and the declaration of the greatness of Mordecai, whereunto the king advanced him, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?"

Modern Corruption

Advancement is pursued as the reward of merit; Scripture says promotion cometh neither from the east nor from the west, and shows Haman miserable at the top.

expand to see more

The reigning account of advancement is meritocratic: a man rises because he is worth it, and if he does not rise he is not. Psalm 75:6-7 denies the premise flatly — promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south. But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another. Samuel says the same of Moses and Aaron. This is not an argument against diligence, which Proverbs commends everywhere, nor a promise that the diligent will always be raised. It relocates the decision. A believer works faithfully in his calling and leaves the setting up and the putting down where it belongs.

Haman is the case study, and his misery is the part usually skipped. He was advanced above all the princes of a world empire, had riches, ten children and a private invitation to the queen's banquet — and he said, yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate. Envy is not cured by elevation; it follows a man up. He went home and built a gallows fifty cubits high, and was hanged on it. The Christian answer is not a better position but a mortified heart, and the discipline for it is the one Paul learned: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'asah (H6213), to make — the LORD who made Moses and Aaron; gadal (H1431), to make great; nasa' (H5375), to lift up.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'asah (H6213) — to do, to make; 1 Samuel 12:6, the LORD that made Moses and Aaron — the margin's reading, and the sense of advancement.

Hebrew gadal (H1431) — to make great, to magnify; Esther 3:1, 5:11, 10:2 — the same verb for Haman's rise and Mordecai's.

Hebrew nasa' (H5375) — to lift, to raise, to bear; Esther 3:1, the king lifted him above all the princes.

Hebrew Agagi (H91) — Agagite; Haman's descent from Agag the Amalekite king Saul spared — an old disobedience returning centuries later.

Greek hupsoo (G5312) — to lift up, to exalt; Luke 14:11, whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.

Usage

"“It is the LORD that advanced Moses and Aaron”."

"“How he had advanced him above the princes” — and it availed him nothing."

"“The greatness of Mordecai, whereunto the king advanced him” — the same verb, reversed."
